title: Things I Need for Serving Others

sections.heading: Remembering who you made us to be
sections.text:
Father, you are the source of every life and every true happiness. You made us able to know you, speak to you, and look for you even in the darkest nights. I worship you for that.

But I also see what sin has done to us. We take the glory you gave us and turn it into shame. We forget you, our Maker, and wander from the very One who gives us life.
theological_themes: God is the Creator and source of true joy; human beings were made for relationship with him, yet sin has bent humanity toward forgetfulness and idolatry.

scripture_references.connection: Paul presents God as the Creator and sustainer of all people, and says human beings were made to seek him. This supports the prayer’s opening confession that life, dependence, and true worship begin in God.
This passage describes humanity’s sinful exchange of God’s glory for created things. It grounds the prayer’s sorrow over human degeneracy and forgetfulness of God.
Elihu speaks of God as the Maker who gives songs in the night. The prayer draws on this image of God as the one people should seek in darkness and distress.

sections.heading: Asking you to awaken what only you can awaken
sections.text:
I know I cannot bring wandering people home by my own strength. Only you can wake the heart, make spiritual things feel real, and keep that awareness from fading away. Every good purpose, every holy desire, every true growth in love and joy comes from you.

You know what is really going on inside me. You know the hidden motives of my heart, and you know my desire to help the gospel spread.
theological_themes: God alone gives spiritual life, conviction, holy desire, and lasting change; ministry depends on divine initiative rather than human ability.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that no one comes to him unless the Father draws him. This directly supports the prayer’s dependence on God to recall wandering people to himself.
Paul says God works in believers both to will and to work for his good pleasure. This grounds the prayer’s claim that good desires and purposes come from God.
This passage teaches that all hearts and motives are exposed before God. It supports the prayer’s honesty that God already knows the secret principles of the soul.

sections.heading: Making me a giver of what you give
sections.text:
Please make me someone who passes on what I have received from you. Let me bring your kindness to people in need, comfort to those whose minds are troubled, healing truth to those sick with sin, hope to people who feel trapped in despair, joy to the grieving, and love to those who have run far from home.

Do not let me serve as if I own any of these gifts. Make me a steward of your mercy, giving freely because everything good has first come from your hand.
theological_themes: Christian service is stewardship: God’s people distribute his mercy, gospel hope, comfort, and love to the poor, suffering, sinful, despairing, and wandering.

scripture_references.connection: Peter describes believers as stewards of God’s varied grace, serving in God’s strength so that God is glorified. This fits the prayer’s request to become a distributor of God’s gifts rather than a self-sufficient helper.
Paul teaches that God entrusts believers with the ministry and message of reconciliation. This supports the prayer’s desire to spread the gospel and call prodigals home.

This passage describes good news for the poor, comfort for the brokenhearted, liberty for captives, and joy for mourners. It illuminates the prayer’s longing to bring God’s help to people in many kinds of need.

sections.heading: Reviving my own cold heart
sections.text:
Holy Spirit, breathe through the ashes of my unbelief. Clear away what is dead and cold in me. Give me light where I am dull, fire where I am lifeless, and the warmth of real love where I am hard.

I need your comfort—not loud or shallow comfort, but the kind that is gentle, quiet, clean, and renewing. Melt my pride. Bring me low before you in the best way, so that I can rest in you as my everything.
theological_themes: The Spirit overcomes unbelief, renews love, brings true comfort, humbles the believer, and teaches the soul to rest in God as all-sufficient.

scripture_references.connection: Paul prays that believers would abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit. This supports the request for the Spirit’s renewing work against unbelief and spiritual coldness.
Paul asks that believers be strengthened by the Spirit and rooted in Christ’s love. This connects closely with the prayer’s plea for inward warmth, love, and spiritual life.
Jesus invites the weary to come to him and find rest under his gentle rule. This grounds the prayer’s longing for peaceful comfort and rest in God rather than self-reliance.

sections.heading: Bearing fruit that blesses others and glorifies you
sections.text:
Make my soul like a garden filled with the wind of your love. Let the life of Christ in me become something others can sense—not for my reputation, but so they are helped and you are honored.

Come and take whatever fruit you grow in me. Let my life do what you made it to do: glorify you and become a blessing to other people.
theological_themes: God’s love produces visible Christian fruit; the goal of the believer’s life and service is God’s glory and the good of others.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that believers bear fruit only by abiding in him, and that such fruit glorifies the Father. This directly supports the prayer’s garden imagery and its desire for God to gather fruit for his glory.
Jesus says good works should lead others to glorify the Father, not the person doing them. This supports the prayer’s aim that visible holiness bless others and honor God.
Paul describes God spreading the fragrance of the knowledge of Christ through his people. This illuminates the prayer’s request that the scent of Christian life be carried to others.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase about giving comfort to the mentally ill reflects an older devotional category that can sound imprecise or stigmatizing today. I rendered it as care for those whose minds are troubled, without implying that mental illness is identical with sin or that it has only spiritual causes.
The phrase “sin-diseased” uses illness as a metaphor for moral and spiritual corruption. I preserved the metaphor while keeping it distinct from the reference to mental distress.

The prayer assumes a strong doctrine of divine initiative in conversion and spiritual renewal, which is central to the Puritan theological setting and can be doctrinally contested among Christians. I preserved that emphasis rather than softening it.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted “almoner” as a steward or distributor of God’s gifts rather than merely someone giving money, because the original list includes gospel comfort, hope, joy, and love as well as help for the indigent.
I treated “songs in the night” as an allusion to Job 35:10 and as an image of seeking God in darkness, not simply as emotional encouragement.

I rendered the garden and fragrance imagery as the visible and perceptible fruit of Christ’s life in the believer, since the original asks that the scents of Christian life be carried to others and that God gather fruit for his glory.
